title: YouTube Music launches new labels as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms
content:
YouTube Music announced Wednesday the rollout of a new labeling system aimed at improving transparency around songs created with the help of generative AI. Now, listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.
The label will appear on the player page. Clicking on this label provides additional information about the specific role of AI in the track’s creation.
Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.
YouTube said it collaborated with various music partners and deployed its own detection tools to identify AI-generated music. According to its help page, partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: “Fully Gen AI,” “Partly Gen AI,” or “No Gen AI.”
“Fully Gen AI” applies to tracks that are entirely generated by AI, while “Partly Gen AI” refers to works where artists may have incorporated AI-generated components but added their own live elements. Tracks edited using pitch-correction tools such as Auto-Tune fall under the “No Gen AI” category.
The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches. For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year. Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.
Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily. The platform labels detected AI-generated music and excludes it from algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists, while also withholding royalties from fraudulent streams. The company is also working on an option to let users filter out AI-generated music.
TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.
YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions. Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization. YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track, which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.

report.summary: YouTube Music introduces AI disclosure labels for tracks, partnering with music labels and using detection tools, as AI-generated music surges across streaming platforms.
report.background: Generative AI music tools such as Suno, Udio, Stable Audio, and YouTube's own Dream Track have made it easy to create realistic songs, leading to a flood of AI-generated tracks on streaming services. Deezer reported receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily. Platforms are responding with varied policies: Apple Music plans Made With AI labels, Spotify has AI labels and a music spam filter, Deezer labels AI music and excludes it from recommendations and royalties, and TIDAL labels and lets users disable it. YouTube is taking a disclosure-first approach, adding labels to YouTube Music and the main YouTube app without banning AI tracks from monetization. The move reflects growing industry and listener pressure for transparency about AI's role in music creation.
key_points: YouTube Music is rolling out AI labels on the player page and main YouTube app. Clicking the label shows more detail about how generative AI was used in composition, vocals, or production.
The system uses three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, and No Gen AI. Tracks using pitch-correction tools like Auto-Tune fall under No Gen AI, which may surprise some listeners.
YouTube relies on partner declarations plus its own detection tools. AI involvement alone does not make a track ineligible for monetization, unlike stricter platforms such as Deezer and TIDAL.
The launch arrives as streaming services race to label AI music. Apple Music, Spotify, Deezer, and TIDAL each have different approaches, from transparency tags to filters and royalty exclusions.
YouTube continues to experiment with AI music creation, including Dream Track, which lets select creators generate soundtracks with AI versions of participating artists' voices.
report.impact: For the AI industry, YouTube's move pushes disclosure toward a mainstream standard, potentially pressuring other platforms to adopt similar labels. It also legitimizes AI music creation while giving listeners more context. Developers will see demand for reliable AI detection, audio watermarking, and metadata standards, creating opportunities in provenance and audio forensics. For regular users, labels offer clearer choices about what they stream, but effectiveness depends on accurate declarations and detection. Artists gain more transparency about AI use, yet monetization remains allowed, so concerns about competition and royalty dilution persist. Overall, the policy favors information over restriction.
report.tools: Follow YouTube Music's AI label help page, Apple Music AI Transparency Tags, Spotify's AI labels and spam filter, Deezer's AI detection and user filter, and TIDAL's AI filter. For open-source exploration, watch Meta's AudioSeal for audio watermarking, Google's SynthID for AI content provenance, and Demucs or Spleeter for audio source separation. Generation tools like MusicGen and AudioCraft help developers understand how AI music is made and detected.
